rows.speaker: Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Zamakhsharī lists several identifications for the people of Rass and gives Shuʿayb’s people as his first preference.
rows.anchor: Zamakhsharī34 has mentioned more names besides referring to the nation of Shu‘ayb (sws). In fact, he has presented the latter as his first preference.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects identifying Rass with Shuʿayb’s people because Qāf distinguishes the people of Rass from the people of Aykah.
rows.anchor: this opinion is not correct in any respect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān identifies the people of Aykah as Shuʿayb’s nation, also stated in the next sūrah, so Rass must be distinct.
rows.anchor: the aṣḥāb al-aykah  refer to nation of Shu‘ayb (sws), as is also

rows.speaker: Sayyid Sulaymān Nadvī
rows.claim: Nadvī identifies the people of Rass as the Qaydamā tribe among the twelve Ishmaelite tribes, while admitting their identity is uncertain.
rows.anchor: Sayyid Sulaymān Nadvī (d. 1953) opines that the aṣḥāb al-rass refer to the Qaydamā tribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage implies that Rass received a messenger, making Nadvī’s Ishmaelite identification difficult because no other Ishmaelite messenger besides Muḥammad is known.
rows.anchor: Here the context in which the aṣḥāb al-rass are mentioned shows a messenger was sent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only a broad identification is supportable: Rass was an ancient Arabian nation to which God sent a messenger.
rows.anchor: they were an ancient nation of Arabia to which God sent a messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Rass denied their messenger and were punished according to God’s established practice.
rows.anchor: they denied him and became worthy of punishment in accordance with the established practice of God.

rows.speaker: Zuhayr
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s quoted line mentions the valley of Rass as a place known in classical poetry.
rows.anchor: Among the classical poets Zuhayr (d. 609 AD) has mentioned the valley of Rass thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān says it has not named every prophet and messenger; God alone knows those left unmentioned.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has specified at various instances that it has not mentioned all prophets and messengers. Those not mentioned are known to God only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historical inquiry has limited scope and contains raw, inauthentic material, so it cannot settle every detail of the past.
rows.anchor: It not only has a limited scope, it is also interspersed with raw and inauthentic data.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows historical events best, so God’s book should be trusted above history; historical corroboration is welcome, while conflict reflects history’s limits.
rows.anchor: Thus instead of books of history, His book must be trusted the most.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression describes explaining something in full detail, including the consequences attached to a warning.
rows.anchor: here connotes explaining something with all its details and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples that portray facts and historical anecdotes are the most effective way to make people understand a matter and its consequences fully.
rows.anchor: the most effective way to do is to use examples that portray facts and employ historical anecdotes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers conclusively convey truth by explaining principles through examples and historical accounts.
rows.anchor: they have not merely confined themselves in putting forth principles. They have also fully explained them through examples and through historical accounts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān explains facts through examples and events so fully that even stubborn people cannot deny them.
rows.anchor: every fact has been explained through examples and events to such an extent that the most stubborn of people cannot deny them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some nations would not understand intellectually and demanded sight; God destroys them through the punishment they denied and demanded to see.
rows.anchor: as per the established practice of God, they are destroyed by the very punishment they deny and demand to see by their eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fully explained the message, but those nations refused it and were routed; the Prophet’s people face the same fate if they fail to value the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: the same fate awaits his people if they do not duly value the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alludes to the settlements of Lot’s people and their destruction, discussed elsewhere in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: This is an allusion to the settlements of Lot’s (sws) people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh caravans passed the ruins of Lot’s people, so the Quraysh could not plead ignorance of the destroyed settlement.
rows.anchor: Their trade caravans pass through routes where the ruins of this nation lie.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh act as if blind to the ruins because they do not expect resurrection after death.
rows.anchor: Since they have no fear of being created again, they pose to be blind about them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in the hereafter grants insight; without it, a person may retain ordinary eyesight but lacks insight.
rows.anchor: a person is blessed with insight if he believes in the hereafter. In the absence of this belief he may have a normal eyesight but will not have insight.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God favored the Quraysh by explaining this life and the next through the Prophet and Qurʾān, but their words show their wretchedness; torment will reveal that the Prophet guided them toward the straight path.
rows.anchor: explaining to them the reality of this world and the next through the Prophet (sws) and the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deviants do not recognize their deviation until they see its outcome; desire enslaves and blinds them to reminders.
rows.anchor: the deviant do not have an idea of their deviance unless they see their fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address form used here is discussed at another point in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: style of address has been discussed at an appropriate instance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses reassure the Prophet: intellect guides, while desire enslaves, and those who abandon intellect cannot be guided.
rows.anchor: It is a person’s intellect that guides him and not his desire. None can guide people who forsake their intellect and become slaves of their desire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Desires are blind and seek only their own fulfillment, without regard for good or evil.
rows.anchor: These desires only want their demands to be fulfilled. They are not concerned with good or evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever makes desire a god becomes caught in Satan’s web in a way that is almost impossible to escape.
rows.anchor: a way that they become his god gets entangled in the web weaved by Satan to such an extent that it become impossible for him to escape from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question addresses the Prophet, who was exerting himself to reform people, and asks whether he expects them still to understand.
rows.anchor: The words “Do you think that most of them hear or understand?” address the Prophet (sws) who was expending all his efforts to reform these people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They have squandered their capacity to understand and become like animals, indeed worse.
rows.anchor: They have wasted away this faculty and now have become animals; in fact, even worse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison is precise rather than hyperbolic: animals follow the instincts God created in them without deviation.
rows.anchor: Animals follow their instincts on which God has created them and do not deviate from them the slightest.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawnan means humility, and salām is both a greeting and a courteous way to depart from someone’s presence.
rows.anchor: The word means “humility.” Just as the word salām is a word of greeting, it is also used

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s salām to his father exemplifies this polite departure.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) said salām to this father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts the arrogant who refused to listen, including those offended by God’s name al-Raḥmān, with the traits of the servants of the Most Merciful.
rows.anchor: they were not ready to even hear it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description both exposes Quraysh leaders’ inner and outer shortcomings and teaches believers the servants’ inward and outward traits and worldly conduct.
rows.anchor: to mirror the glory and majesty of human character before these arrogant leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humility is named first because of the occasion and context.
rows.anchor: Here, in due deference to the occasion and context, the first trait mentioned is “humility.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A humble gait reflects the inner self and expresses awe before God’s power and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: A humble gait actually reflects the inner- self. The real purpose is to point to the fact they are so over-awed by the power and sovereignty of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogance appears in a person’s actions generally and especially in the way he walks.
rows.anchor: When a person has arrogance in him, it is evident in every action of his but it specially manifests itself in his gait.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Submission to truth makes one a servant of the Most Merciful even with a proud gait, while rebellion makes one Satan’s companion despite a humble gait.
rows.anchor: If a person submits to every truth, whether big or small, that comes his way, he is included among the servants of the Most Merciful God even if he walks proudly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogance follows Satan’s way and prevents any virtue from taking root.
rows.anchor: arrogance is the way of Satan and such is the nature of this evil that no virtue can be nurtured in a person in its presence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhāṭabah means engaging in an argument.
rows.anchor: The word ﻣﺨﺎﻃﺒﻪ means to indulge in an argument.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ignorant are uncouth, ill-mannered mockers of the Prophet’s servants; the servants avoid entanglement and leave with Abraham’s polite salām.
rows.anchor: they do not entangle themselves with them and leave their company by following the way of Abraham (sws) and saying salām to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salām politely dismisses such people; withdrawal may prompt someone with virtue to reconsider and listen rather than argue.
rows.anchor: If a person withdraws from such people in such a manner, it can be hoped that if there is any semblance of virtue in him, he will review his attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a person seeks only argument and dispute, the servants of the Most Merciful should not talk with him.
rows.anchor: if there is no such thing found in a person and the only thing he is after is argument and dispute, then it is not befitting for the servants of the Most Merciful God to talk to him.
